medical.title: High anxiety may alter the brain's sleep switch in preteens
medical.summary: Some preteens have no trouble getting a full night's rest. Those experiencing anxiety often lie awake. The reason for both may be related to a pea-sized gland in the middle of their brains.

medical.title: Occupational therapy generated health care savings for primary care patients with diabetes
medical.summary: According to a new randomized study of primary care patients with diabetes, those who received Lifestyle Redesign occupational therapy generated more than $250,000 in health care cost savings compared with patients who received usual care alone.

medical.title: Does thin air slow the mind? New research on skiers' mental reactions
medical.summary: In mogul skiing, a fraction of a second can make all the difference. A momentary lapse in attention, a misjudged turn or a delayed decision can turn a smooth sequence into a mistake or even a disaster.

medical.title: Moving the needle on lung cancer screenings: Medical students work with researchers to improve outcomes
medical.summary: Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer death in the United States, claiming more than 125,000 lives each year. There is a quick, painless screening test that can detect lung cancer before symptoms appear, when treatment is more effective. Yet more than 80% of those eligible for a low-dose CT scan (LDCT) never get screened.

medical.title: Newly mapped brain circuit offers clues to how slow nasal breathing eases anxiety
medical.summary: A slow breath in and out does the trick for many people when calming their nerves and dealing with anxiety, a disorder that affects millions of people worldwide. Pranayama, Taoism and meditation have long used slow nasal breathing to ease a negative mood. How this simple act works its magic, however, has been tickling the gray cells of scientists curious to unravel the biological pathways behind it. Now, scientists may have found a clue.

medical.title: Vaping additives weaken key lung film at higher concentrations, lab tests suggest
medical.summary: A new study from the University of Kansas shows that additives common in commercially available vaping devices, such as vitamin E and CBD, soften a vital lung surfactant at high enough concentrations, at least in a simplified lab model.

medical.title: Immune protein loss may drive rare stomach lymphoma in H. pylori infections
medical.summary: Roughly half the world's population is infected with the stomach bacterium Helicobacter pylori, which is responsible for about 90% of gastric cancers. However, until now, it has been unclear why some H. pylori infections lead to a rare form of lymphoma in the stomach while others don't.

medical.title: Analysis links COVID-19 infection in unvaccinated people to lower subsequent type 1 diabetes risk
medical.summary: New research presented at the Annual Meeting of the European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD) in Milan, Italy, shows that people who have had COVID-19 have a lower, rather than higher, risk of subsequently developing type 1 diabetes (T1D).

medical.title: Scientists find a bone-building switch that could fight osteoporosis
medical.summary: An experimental compound called AP503 significantly strengthened bones in mice by activating GPR133, a receptor that boosts bone formation while slowing bone loss. Because the same treatment has also been linked to stronger muscles, researchers see intriguing potential for combating age-related decline and osteoporosis.

medical.title: Immunity for the long haul: Why some antibodies are built to last
medical.summary: When an infection strikes, the immune system produces antibodies to help fight it off. Some antibody responses can protect us for years, while others fade much sooner. Using a mouse model, a team of researchers led by The University of Osaka, uncovered several ways cells that produce IgG1, a subclass of IgG antibody commonly associated with long-lasting immune responses, might help establish lasting immune protection. The study is published in the journal Science Immunology.

medical.title: Not all colonoscopies are the same: New AI audits them at scale
medical.summary: Colonoscopies are one of the most effective ways to prevent colorectal cancer, which is surging among young adults in the U.S. Yet, the quality of each procedure can vary substantially from one physician to another. As a result, medical societies recommend routinely reviewing every colonoscopist—something that's challenging and time-consuming for practices to implement.

medical.title: The market forces quietly adding thousands to patient bills
medical.summary: Health care integration is occurring at a breakneck pace across the U.S., with endless permutations: Hospitals are buying doctors' practices and surgery and imaging centers. Insurers are buying doctors' practices and specialty pharmacies and sometimes merging with pharmacy chains. Hospitals are buying or creating insurers.

medical.title: Nasal spray protects neurons and memory in Alzheimer's mouse model
medical.summary: A nasal spray containing vesicles naturally released by cells may work against Alzheimer's. This is the promise of a study conducted by researchers at the Università Cattolica, Fondazione Policlinico Universitario A. Gemelli IRCCS, and the E. Menni Research Center of Fondazione Poliambulanza.

medical.title: Bacterial trial fails to demonstrate early asthma prevention
medical.summary: A national clinical trial led by researchers at the University of Arizona College of Medicine—Tucson found that treating young children with an oral bacterial extract did not reduce the risk of severe wheezing and respiratory illnesses that can precede asthma.

medical.title: Study finds limited evidence for helping hospitalized patients with alcohol use disorder connect to follow-up care
medical.summary: A systematic review by researchers at the University of Colorado Anschutz and Yale University found limited evidence that hospital-based interventions can help people with alcohol use disorder connect with outpatient treatment after they leave the hospital.

medical.title: Study finds social, financial and health care factors shape resilience in adults with sickle cell disease
medical.summary: A study published in the Journal of Sickle Cell Disease by researchers at Binghamton University's Decker College of Nursing and Health Sciences explored how individual and community health experiences of adults with sickle cell disease (SCD) shape resilience—the capacity to adapt to adversity.

medical.title: Researchers identify risk factors for dementia among American Indians
medical.summary: In a study in the journal Alzheimer's & Dementia, researchers detected significant risk associations for vascular and Alzheimer's dementias among American Indians for four previously identified key risk factors: limited education, hypertension, social isolation and depression.

medical.title: Study finds longer periods of air pollution exposure can stress the heart
medical.summary: As the heat of late summer leads to increased air quality alerts, those with cardiovascular conditions or who are outdoors for long periods may want to take note. University of Louisville researchers have discovered that longer exposure to air pollution has measurable negative effects on the heart and overall health.

medical.title: Algorithmic tool may improve screening of patients for an Alzheimer's clinical trial
medical.summary: A new blood-based screening algorithm dramatically reduced the number of unnecessary PET scans needed to recruit patients at risk of Alzheimer's disease for a clinical trial, according to research from scientists at the Keck School of Medicine of USC published in the journal Alzheimer's & Dementia.

medical.title: ‘My life-changing career break happened because I was wearing a second hand coat’
medical.summary: Richard E Grant struck gold in a charity shop – now he’s fronting a camping to inspire others to do the same The post ‘My life-changing career break happened because I was wearing a second hand coat’ appeared first on Positive News .

medical.title: How London’s low emissions zone is helping children breathe easier
medical.summary: Seven years on from London’s low emission zone, researchers are measuring its impact on health – with striking results for children’s lungs The post How London’s low emissions zone is helping children breathe easier appeared first on Positive News .

science.title: How 'parachute science' is failing the world's tropical insects
science.summary: Monash University scientists have developed a global framework to tackle a major blind spot in biodiversity conservation: Insects underpin ecosystems and food production but remain largely invisible to conservation efforts across the tropics.

science.title: Reading app boosts kids' literacy
science.summary: A new Flinders University study of primary school children shows a science-based digital phonics reading app can accelerate early reading while helping teachers quickly identify students needing extra support.

science.title: A 66.5-million-year-old trackway captures adult T. rex at walking pace
science.summary: Scientists from the Denver Museum of Nature & Science and Liverpool John Moores University in England have discovered the first adult T. rex trackway, providing insights into how this emblematic predator moved. The findings are published in the Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology.

science.title: Anak Krakatau erupts, disrupting 300,000 travelers as 1883 disaster looms large
science.summary: Indonesia's Mount Anak Krakatau has erupted again this week, sending plumes of volcanic ash high into the sky and disrupting hundreds of flights. More than 300,000 passengers have been affected.

science.title: Ancient DNA reveals 1,000 years of human-environment interactions at Crawford Lake
science.summary: An international team of scientists has recreated a 1,000-year timeline documenting ecological changes and human impact on the area surrounding Crawford Lake, the famed location of the proposed Anthropocene.

science.title: Heat forces French Champagne makers to stiffen their drink
science.summary: Drinking this year's champagne might cause a heftier headache as France's record heat waves force some producers to increase alcohol levels, industry officials said Wednesday.

science.title: Ancient bones reveal that cannibalism took different forms in Neolithic Spain
science.summary: Cannibalism was sometimes on the Neolithic menu, as numerous archaeological discoveries have revealed. But while ancient human bones show the practice took place, far less evidence exists about the forms it may have taken or why people occasionally consumed one another. Was it to stave off hunger during times of desperation? Did different tribes eat their defeated enemies? Or was cannibalism part of complex rituals?

science.title: Could quantum protocols make electronic voting more secure?
science.summary: Electronic voting, the use of electronic systems to cast, record or count votes, could potentially simplify the process of electing new political leaders or other representatives. While some countries have already started using internet-connected devices or electronic voting machines at polling stations, the trustworthiness, security and anonymity of electronic voting systems are still widely debated.

science.title: Soft X-ray absorption spectroscopy of organic molecules in organic solvents for applying organic reactions
science.summary: In research published in the journal Physical Chemistry Chemical Physics, the electronic structures of organic molecules containing sp2-hybridized carbons in organic solvents were studied using C K-edge X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS), termed "Soft-XAS-OS."

science.title: NASA Names Two Artemis II Astronauts to Emeritus Program
science.summary: Following their landmark Artemis II mission earlier this year, distinguished NASA astronauts Victor Glover and Reid Wiseman are transitioning in September to emeritus status at the agency’s Johnson Space Center in Houston. In an emeritus role, individuals with a high degree of technical and professional knowledge can continue to support the agency by donating their […]

science.title: Study into career shocks finds what doesn't break expats makes them stronger
science.summary: New research challenges the idea that career shocks are bad news for expatriate workers, finding that major personal, professional or societal disruptions can instead act as a catalyst for adaptation and resilience.

science.title: Biologists find a hidden weak spot in how bacteria build the tails they use to move
science.summary: New research from Indiana University has uncovered a previously unknown vulnerability in how bacteria build the whip-like tails they use to move. The researchers found that building these tails can put stress on the protective wall surrounding a bacterial cell and uncovered systems bacteria use to keep that stress from becoming destructive.

science.title: Pounding waves open up sinkhole in swanky Malibu
science.summary: Pounding surf lashing the swanky California enclave of Malibu on Tuesday opened a giant sinkhole in the driveway of a house reportedly belonging to U.S. actor Nicolas Cage.

science.title: Local microbes persist in wine despite commercial yeast
science.summary: A new study has demonstrated that regional microbial imprints can remain detectable under commercial winemaking conditions. The research, appearing in Applied and Environmental Microbiology, shows that inoculated fermentations do not "override" native microbial diversity and that vineyard management and environmental conditions affect wine quality. The study helps explain why wines from different regions taste distinct even when made with similar techniques and supports regional flavors and branding.

science.title: Canada eyes researchers looking to leave 'hostile' US
science.summary: Fed up with funding restrictions surrounding her research on links between climate change and health, American epidemiologist Sheryl Magzamen has left the United States for Canada.

science.title: Can a messy person become a tidy person? Or are we doomed?
science.summary: Some people seem naturally tidy. Their keys are always in the same place, clothes make it into the closet, and their kitchen counter remains mysteriously visible.

science.title: Some police officers use the 'bad guys' label to provide moral clarity
science.summary: A new study shows that some U.S. police officers often use the term "bad guys" to describe people who commit crimes, especially when faced with ambiguity in their work. It is a label officers may use to reduce complex and morally challenging situations and contexts into a clearer, more legible framework.

science.title: A wandering black hole caught feeding on the run
science.summary: Astronomers have found the first direct evidence that a wandering black hole can feed itself by dragging gas along in its wake as it moves through its galaxy. It's the first direct evidence of an accretion channel long predicted in theory but never before observed. The paper describing this discovery was posted to the arXiv preprint server on Aug. 11.

science.title: Researchers discuss how data center construction could influence voters and impact public land
science.summary: The construction of new data centers is shaping up to be a defining issue in the 2026 midterm elections. Politicians in both parties have been distancing themselves from data centers in the face of public discontent around the issue, with public backlash leading to the freezing of dozens of data center projects nationwide this year.

science.title: Have we found alien life? Hundreds of scientists weigh in
science.summary: Two major alien-life announcements in 2025 generated enormous excitement, but most astrobiologists remained unconvinced. Only 6.6% of surveyed experts thought possible biological molecules on K2-18b probably represented extraterrestrial life, while 15.1% said the same about intriguing mineral patterns in a Martian rock.

science.title: OpenAI says 10,000 AI agents cracked one of math's hardest problems in 88 hours
science.summary: OpenAI said Tuesday that one of its unreleased artificial intelligence models had solved a mathematical puzzle that has eluded mathematicians for generations, a claim that also drew a fight with rival researchers over credit.

science.title: Interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS is bursting with methanol
science.summary: Interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS contains exceptionally high levels of methanol, suggesting it formed under conditions very different from those that shaped most comets in our solar system. ALMA also revealed that tiny icy grains around the comet are releasing methanol like miniature comets, giving astronomers an unusually detailed look at an object from another star system.

science.title: Devil’s Arrows: Ancient builders hauled 55,000-pound stones 11 miles for Britain’s tallest stone row
science.summary: Britain’s towering Devil’s Arrows were built from 25-tonne stones hauled at least 18 kilometers from Brimham Rocks around 4,000 years ago. The discovery reveals an astonishing feat of prehistoric engineering and suggests the stones’ distant source may have been chosen for cultural or spiritual reasons.

science.title: “Parachute science” is failing the tropics, home to more than 80% of insect species
science.summary: Insects quietly hold much of the natural world together, yet conservation efforts are overlooking the tropical regions where more than 80 percent of insect species live. Monash University researchers have developed a global framework to close this gap by combining scientific studies with museum collections, local expertise, citizen science, social media records, and new technologies.

environment.title: Galaxy Gallery: Galactic Gems Glisten in New Gallery From NASA’s Chandra
environment.summary: This gallery displays a collection of 16 galactic images from Chandra and other telescopes. Astronomers put galaxies into three main categories: spirals like our own Milky Way, ellipticals that are older and likely the results of mergers, and irregulars that can encompass a wide range of galactic phenomena. All types are represented in this collection. Each galactic image contains X-ray data from Chandra combined with data from telescopes such as NASA’s Webb, Hubble, IXPE, Swift, and NuSTAR, and others both in space and on the ground. The post Galaxy Gallery: Galactic Gems Glisten in New Gallery From NASA’s Chandra appeared first on NASA Science .

environment.title: A Manhattan-sized ice island just broke free from Greenland
environment.summary: A huge section of Greenland’s Petermann Glacier has snapped off, forming an ice island about the size of Manhattan. Satellites watched cracks spread rapidly before the 76-square-kilometer slab finally broke free on August 4. It is the glacier’s biggest calving event since 2012, and scientists say two even larger pieces could eventually follow. The rare Arctic iceberg will now be tracked as it drifts, breaks apart, and potentially affects shipping routes.

environment.title: Atomic catalyst unlocks the hidden value of plant waste
environment.summary: Scientists have created a highly efficient catalyst that breaks down stubborn lignin from plant waste into useful chemicals under relatively mild conditions. By revealing exactly how the catalyst works at the atomic level, the discovery could help turn forestry and agricultural waste into renewable building blocks for fuels, plastics, and other materials.

environment.title: Scientists find hidden “highways” guiding animal evolution
environment.summary: A sweeping analysis of thousands of animal genomes suggests that chromosomes do not evolve randomly but instead follow a limited number of irreversible “evolutionary highways.” These one-way genetic changes preserve clues to more than 600 million years of animal history and could even help researchers explore where evolution may head next.

environment.title: NASA finds Earth microbes could survive on the Moon
environment.summary: NASA scientists found that microbes brought by astronauts could survive in cold, shadowed niches around the Moon’s South Pole, potentially complicating future searches for pristine lunar chemistry. Some refuges may be no larger than a footprint, while one hardy fungus could even withstand limited exposure to sunlight.

mix_items.summary: Monash University scientists have developed a global framework to tackle a major blind spot in biodiversity conservation: Insects underpin ecosystems and food production but remain largely invisible to conservation efforts across the tropics.

mix_items.title: Does thin air slow the mind? New research on skiers' mental reactions
mix_items.summary: In mogul skiing, a fraction of a second can make all the difference. A momentary lapse in attention, a misjudged turn or a delayed decision can turn a smooth sequence into a mistake or even a disaster.

mix_items.title: Moving the needle on lung cancer screenings: Medical students work with researchers to improve outcomes
mix_items.summary: Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer death in the United States, claiming more than 125,000 lives each year. There is a quick, painless screening test that can detect lung cancer before symptoms appear, when treatment is more effective. Yet more than 80% of those eligible for a low-dose CT scan (LDCT) never get screened.

mix_items.title: Reading app boosts kids' literacy
mix_items.summary: A new Flinders University study of primary school children shows a science-based digital phonics reading app can accelerate early reading while helping teachers quickly identify students needing extra support.

mix_items.title: A 66.5-million-year-old trackway captures adult T. rex at walking pace
mix_items.summary: Scientists from the Denver Museum of Nature & Science and Liverpool John Moores University in England have discovered the first adult T. rex trackway, providing insights into how this emblematic predator moved. The findings are published in the Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology.

mix_items.title: Newly mapped brain circuit offers clues to how slow nasal breathing eases anxiety
mix_items.summary: A slow breath in and out does the trick for many people when calming their nerves and dealing with anxiety, a disorder that affects millions of people worldwide. Pranayama, Taoism and meditation have long used slow nasal breathing to ease a negative mood. How this simple act works its magic, however, has been tickling the gray cells of scientists curious to unravel the biological pathways behind it. Now, scientists may have found a clue.

mix_items.title: Anak Krakatau erupts, disrupting 300,000 travelers as 1883 disaster looms large
mix_items.summary: Indonesia's Mount Anak Krakatau has erupted again this week, sending plumes of volcanic ash high into the sky and disrupting hundreds of flights. More than 300,000 passengers have been affected.

mix_items.title: Vaping additives weaken key lung film at higher concentrations, lab tests suggest
mix_items.summary: A new study from the University of Kansas shows that additives common in commercially available vaping devices, such as vitamin E and CBD, soften a vital lung surfactant at high enough concentrations, at least in a simplified lab model.

mix_items.title: Immune protein loss may drive rare stomach lymphoma in H. pylori infections
mix_items.summary: Roughly half the world's population is infected with the stomach bacterium Helicobacter pylori, which is responsible for about 90% of gastric cancers. However, until now, it has been unclear why some H. pylori infections lead to a rare form of lymphoma in the stomach while others don't.

mix_items.title: Analysis links COVID-19 infection in unvaccinated people to lower subsequent type 1 diabetes risk
mix_items.summary: New research presented at the Annual Meeting of the European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD) in Milan, Italy, shows that people who have had COVID-19 have a lower, rather than higher, risk of subsequently developing type 1 diabetes (T1D).

mix_items.title: Ancient DNA reveals 1,000 years of human-environment interactions at Crawford Lake
mix_items.summary: An international team of scientists has recreated a 1,000-year timeline documenting ecological changes and human impact on the area surrounding Crawford Lake, the famed location of the proposed Anthropocene.

mix_items.title: Heat forces French Champagne makers to stiffen their drink
mix_items.summary: Drinking this year's champagne might cause a heftier headache as France's record heat waves force some producers to increase alcohol levels, industry officials said Wednesday.

mix_items.title: Scientists find a bone-building switch that could fight osteoporosis
mix_items.summary: An experimental compound called AP503 significantly strengthened bones in mice by activating GPR133, a receptor that boosts bone formation while slowing bone loss. Because the same treatment has also been linked to stronger muscles, researchers see intriguing potential for combating age-related decline and osteoporosis.

mix_items.title: Ancient bones reveal that cannibalism took different forms in Neolithic Spain
mix_items.summary: Cannibalism was sometimes on the Neolithic menu, as numerous archaeological discoveries have revealed. But while ancient human bones show the practice took place, far less evidence exists about the forms it may have taken or why people occasionally consumed one another. Was it to stave off hunger during times of desperation? Did different tribes eat their defeated enemies? Or was cannibalism part of complex rituals?

mix_items.title: Could quantum protocols make electronic voting more secure?
mix_items.summary: Electronic voting, the use of electronic systems to cast, record or count votes, could potentially simplify the process of electing new political leaders or other representatives. While some countries have already started using internet-connected devices or electronic voting machines at polling stations, the trustworthiness, security and anonymity of electronic voting systems are still widely debated.

mix_items.title: Soft X-ray absorption spectroscopy of organic molecules in organic solvents for applying organic reactions
mix_items.summary: In research published in the journal Physical Chemistry Chemical Physics, the electronic structures of organic molecules containing sp2-hybridized carbons in organic solvents were studied using C K-edge X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS), termed "Soft-XAS-OS."

mix_items.title: Immunity for the long haul: Why some antibodies are built to last
mix_items.summary: When an infection strikes, the immune system produces antibodies to help fight it off. Some antibody responses can protect us for years, while others fade much sooner. Using a mouse model, a team of researchers led by The University of Osaka, uncovered several ways cells that produce IgG1, a subclass of IgG antibody commonly associated with long-lasting immune responses, might help establish lasting immune protection. The study is published in the journal Science Immunology.

mix_items.title: NASA Names Two Artemis II Astronauts to Emeritus Program
mix_items.summary: Following their landmark Artemis II mission earlier this year, distinguished NASA astronauts Victor Glover and Reid Wiseman are transitioning in September to emeritus status at the agency’s Johnson Space Center in Houston. In an emeritus role, individuals with a high degree of technical and professional knowledge can continue to support the agency by donating their […]

mix_items.title: Study into career shocks finds what doesn't break expats makes them stronger
mix_items.summary: New research challenges the idea that career shocks are bad news for expatriate workers, finding that major personal, professional or societal disruptions can instead act as a catalyst for adaptation and resilience.

mix_items.title: Not all colonoscopies are the same: New AI audits them at scale
mix_items.summary: Colonoscopies are one of the most effective ways to prevent colorectal cancer, which is surging among young adults in the U.S. Yet, the quality of each procedure can vary substantially from one physician to another. As a result, medical societies recommend routinely reviewing every colonoscopist—something that's challenging and time-consuming for practices to implement.

mix_items.title: The market forces quietly adding thousands to patient bills
mix_items.summary: Health care integration is occurring at a breakneck pace across the U.S., with endless permutations: Hospitals are buying doctors' practices and surgery and imaging centers. Insurers are buying doctors' practices and specialty pharmacies and sometimes merging with pharmacy chains. Hospitals are buying or creating insurers.

mix_items.title: Biologists find a hidden weak spot in how bacteria build the tails they use to move
mix_items.summary: New research from Indiana University has uncovered a previously unknown vulnerability in how bacteria build the whip-like tails they use to move. The researchers found that building these tails can put stress on the protective wall surrounding a bacterial cell and uncovered systems bacteria use to keep that stress from becoming destructive.

mix_items.title: Pounding waves open up sinkhole in swanky Malibu
mix_items.summary: Pounding surf lashing the swanky California enclave of Malibu on Tuesday opened a giant sinkhole in the driveway of a house reportedly belonging to U.S. actor Nicolas Cage.

mix_items.title: Local microbes persist in wine despite commercial yeast
mix_items.summary: A new study has demonstrated that regional microbial imprints can remain detectable under commercial winemaking conditions. The research, appearing in Applied and Environmental Microbiology, shows that inoculated fermentations do not "override" native microbial diversity and that vineyard management and environmental conditions affect wine quality. The study helps explain why wines from different regions taste distinct even when made with similar techniques and supports regional flavors and branding.

mix_items.title: Nasal spray protects neurons and memory in Alzheimer's mouse model
mix_items.summary: A nasal spray containing vesicles naturally released by cells may work against Alzheimer's. This is the promise of a study conducted by researchers at the Università Cattolica, Fondazione Policlinico Universitario A. Gemelli IRCCS, and the E. Menni Research Center of Fondazione Poliambulanza.

mix_items.title: Bacterial trial fails to demonstrate early asthma prevention
mix_items.summary: A national clinical trial led by researchers at the University of Arizona College of Medicine—Tucson found that treating young children with an oral bacterial extract did not reduce the risk of severe wheezing and respiratory illnesses that can precede asthma.

mix_items.title: Canada eyes researchers looking to leave 'hostile' US
mix_items.summary: Fed up with funding restrictions surrounding her research on links between climate change and health, American epidemiologist Sheryl Magzamen has left the United States for Canada.

mix_items.title: Study finds limited evidence for helping hospitalized patients with alcohol use disorder connect to follow-up care
mix_items.summary: A systematic review by researchers at the University of Colorado Anschutz and Yale University found limited evidence that hospital-based interventions can help people with alcohol use disorder connect with outpatient treatment after they leave the hospital.

mix_items.title: Can a messy person become a tidy person? Or are we doomed?
mix_items.summary: Some people seem naturally tidy. Their keys are always in the same place, clothes make it into the closet, and their kitchen counter remains mysteriously visible.

mix_items.title: Study finds social, financial and health care factors shape resilience in adults with sickle cell disease
mix_items.summary: A study published in the Journal of Sickle Cell Disease by researchers at Binghamton University's Decker College of Nursing and Health Sciences explored how individual and community health experiences of adults with sickle cell disease (SCD) shape resilience—the capacity to adapt to adversity.

mix_items.title: Some police officers use the 'bad guys' label to provide moral clarity
mix_items.summary: A new study shows that some U.S. police officers often use the term "bad guys" to describe people who commit crimes, especially when faced with ambiguity in their work. It is a label officers may use to reduce complex and morally challenging situations and contexts into a clearer, more legible framework.

mix_items.title: Researchers identify risk factors for dementia among American Indians
mix_items.summary: In a study in the journal Alzheimer's & Dementia, researchers detected significant risk associations for vascular and Alzheimer's dementias among American Indians for four previously identified key risk factors: limited education, hypertension, social isolation and depression.

mix_items.title: A wandering black hole caught feeding on the run
mix_items.summary: Astronomers have found the first direct evidence that a wandering black hole can feed itself by dragging gas along in its wake as it moves through its galaxy. It's the first direct evidence of an accretion channel long predicted in theory but never before observed. The paper describing this discovery was posted to the arXiv preprint server on Aug. 11.

mix_items.title: Study finds longer periods of air pollution exposure can stress the heart
mix_items.summary: As the heat of late summer leads to increased air quality alerts, those with cardiovascular conditions or who are outdoors for long periods may want to take note. University of Louisville researchers have discovered that longer exposure to air pollution has measurable negative effects on the heart and overall health.

mix_items.title: Researchers discuss how data center construction could influence voters and impact public land
mix_items.summary: The construction of new data centers is shaping up to be a defining issue in the 2026 midterm elections. Politicians in both parties have been distancing themselves from data centers in the face of public discontent around the issue, with public backlash leading to the freezing of dozens of data center projects nationwide this year.

mix_items.title: Have we found alien life? Hundreds of scientists weigh in
mix_items.summary: Two major alien-life announcements in 2025 generated enormous excitement, but most astrobiologists remained unconvinced. Only 6.6% of surveyed experts thought possible biological molecules on K2-18b probably represented extraterrestrial life, while 15.1% said the same about intriguing mineral patterns in a Martian rock.

mix_items.title: Algorithmic tool may improve screening of patients for an Alzheimer's clinical trial
mix_items.summary: A new blood-based screening algorithm dramatically reduced the number of unnecessary PET scans needed to recruit patients at risk of Alzheimer's disease for a clinical trial, according to research from scientists at the Keck School of Medicine of USC published in the journal Alzheimer's & Dementia.

mix_items.title: OpenAI says 10,000 AI agents cracked one of math's hardest problems in 88 hours
mix_items.summary: OpenAI said Tuesday that one of its unreleased artificial intelligence models had solved a mathematical puzzle that has eluded mathematicians for generations, a claim that also drew a fight with rival researchers over credit.

mix_items.title: Interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS is bursting with methanol
mix_items.summary: Interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS contains exceptionally high levels of methanol, suggesting it formed under conditions very different from those that shaped most comets in our solar system. ALMA also revealed that tiny icy grains around the comet are releasing methanol like miniature comets, giving astronomers an unusually detailed look at an object from another star system.

mix_items.title: Devil’s Arrows: Ancient builders hauled 55,000-pound stones 11 miles for Britain’s tallest stone row
mix_items.summary: Britain’s towering Devil’s Arrows were built from 25-tonne stones hauled at least 18 kilometers from Brimham Rocks around 4,000 years ago. The discovery reveals an astonishing feat of prehistoric engineering and suggests the stones’ distant source may have been chosen for cultural or spiritual reasons.

mix_items.title: “Parachute science” is failing the tropics, home to more than 80% of insect species
mix_items.summary: Insects quietly hold much of the natural world together, yet conservation efforts are overlooking the tropical regions where more than 80 percent of insect species live. Monash University researchers have developed a global framework to close this gap by combining scientific studies with museum collections, local expertise, citizen science, social media records, and new technologies.

mix_items.title: Marine conservation collides with mining in Indonesia’s biodiversity-rich Moramo Bay
mix_items.summary: SOUTH KONAWE, Indonesia — A marine protected area in Indonesia’s Southeast Sulawesi province is home to a critically depleted population of humphead wrasse. The species presence helped the area gain its protected status, but mining permits overlap parts of the conservation zone and line its coast. mix_items.title: Galaxy Gallery: Galactic Gems Glisten in New Gallery From NASA’s Chandra
mix_items.summary: This gallery displays a collection of 16 galactic images from Chandra and other telescopes. Astronomers put galaxies into three main categories: spirals like our own Milky Way, ellipticals that are older and likely the results of mergers, and irregulars that can encompass a wide range of galactic phenomena. All types are represented in this collection. Each galactic image contains X-ray data from Chandra combined with data from telescopes such as NASA’s Webb, Hubble, IXPE, Swift, and NuSTAR, and others both in space and on the ground. The post Galaxy Gallery: Galactic Gems Glisten in New Gallery From NASA’s Chandra appeared first on NASA Science .

mix_items.title: A Manhattan-sized ice island just broke free from Greenland
mix_items.summary: A huge section of Greenland’s Petermann Glacier has snapped off, forming an ice island about the size of Manhattan. Satellites watched cracks spread rapidly before the 76-square-kilometer slab finally broke free on August 4. It is the glacier’s biggest calving event since 2012, and scientists say two even larger pieces could eventually follow. The rare Arctic iceberg will now be tracked as it drifts, breaks apart, and potentially affects shipping routes.

mix_items.title: Atomic catalyst unlocks the hidden value of plant waste
mix_items.summary: Scientists have created a highly efficient catalyst that breaks down stubborn lignin from plant waste into useful chemicals under relatively mild conditions. By revealing exactly how the catalyst works at the atomic level, the discovery could help turn forestry and agricultural waste into renewable building blocks for fuels, plastics, and other materials.

mix_items.title: Scientists find hidden “highways” guiding animal evolution
mix_items.summary: A sweeping analysis of thousands of animal genomes suggests that chromosomes do not evolve randomly but instead follow a limited number of irreversible “evolutionary highways.” These one-way genetic changes preserve clues to more than 600 million years of animal history and could even help researchers explore where evolution may head next.

mix_items.title: NASA finds Earth microbes could survive on the Moon
mix_items.summary: NASA scientists found that microbes brought by astronauts could survive in cold, shadowed niches around the Moon’s South Pole, potentially complicating future searches for pristine lunar chemistry. Some refuges may be no larger than a footprint, while one hardy fungus could even withstand limited exposure to sunlight.
